  • demo/api/src/lgos_demo_api/graphs/ contains its graphs and adapters.
  • demo/api-coding-agent/src/lgos_api_coding_agent/ owns the separately deployed coding-agent showcase, currently backed by Codex.

Continue with Run the Demo API for request examples or Chainlit and Open WebUI for UI behavior.

items.title: Background Interrupt
items.text:
background-interrupt demonstrates deterministic background execution, human review, and background resumption. It prepares a mock report, always asks for approval, and finishes only after approval. It calls no model and performs no external action. Hatchet executes background requests; PostgreSQL preserves the paused graph and coordinates execution across the API and worker processes.

Use background-mock for basic polling and cancellation, or deep-research for a real agent that combines background execution with reviewed work.

items.title: LangGraph Topology
items.text:
graph TD;
    __start__ --> prepare_report;
    prepare_report --> review_report;
    review_report --> finish_report;
    finish_report --> __end__;

items.title: Request Flow
items.text:
Select background-interrupt and enable Run in background before sending the prompt. Keep the switch enabled when answering the review so the continuation also runs in the worker. Selecting the model alone does not enable background execution.

The UI's API calls below pass through the selected gateway. Hatchet / worker combines the job service and its independent worker. R1 and R2 label two different Response IDs belonging to one graph workflow.

sequenceDiagram
  participant UI as Chainlit / Open WebUI
  participant API as LGOS API
  participant Jobs as Hatchet / worker
  participant DB as PostgreSQL

  Note over UI: User enables background<br/>and sends a prompt
  UI->>API: responses.create<br/>background=true
  API->>Jobs: Queue preparation
  API-->>UI: queued Response R1
  par Worker prepares and pauses
    Jobs->>Jobs: Delay, then prepare report
    Jobs->>DB: Checkpoint at review
    Jobs->>Jobs: Store completed R1<br/>with lgos_interrupt
  and UI polls R1 until terminal
    loop Until R1 completes
      UI->>API: responses.retrieve(R1)
      API->>Jobs: Read status and output
      API-->>UI: queued / in_progress,<br/>then completed with review call
    end
  end
  UI->>UI: Show report and<br/>Approve / Reject choices
  Note over Jobs,DB: Graph paused in PostgreSQL<br/>no worker waits for the answer
  Note over UI: User approves or rejects
  UI->>API: responses.create<br/>background=true<br/>previous_response_id=R1<br/>function_call_output with answer
  API->>Jobs: Queue continuation
  API-->>UI: queued Response R2
  Jobs->>DB: Acquire lease and<br/>load pending checkpoint
  Jobs->>Jobs: Resume review_report<br/>with the answer
  alt Approve
    Jobs->>Jobs: Delay, then return report
  else Reject
    Jobs->>Jobs: Return rejection<br/>without delay
  end
  Jobs->>DB: Clean up terminal checkpoint
  Jobs->>Jobs: Store completed R2<br/>with final answer
  loop Poll R2 until terminal
    UI->>API: responses.retrieve(R2)
    API->>Jobs: Read status and output
    API-->>UI: queued / in_progress,<br/>then completed with answer
  end
  UI->>UI: Show final report or rejection

At review, R1 is completed while the graph is paused. Resuming creates R2; polling R1 again continues to return the original review call. There is no separate paused Response status. The answer uses the exact call_id from R1 in a function_call_output item. For the exact SDK fields, see Python SDK example.

items.title: Cancellation
items.text:
The outcome depends on whether a background Response is still active:

flowchart TD
  cancel["User requests cancellation"] --> stage{"When?"}
  stage -->|"Preparing R1 or finishing R2"| active["UI requests cancellation of the current Response ID"]
  active --> stopped["Request Hatchet cancellation; result is cancelled unless already terminal"]
  stage -->|"Waiting for review"| review["R1 is already completed; cancelling R1 returns it unchanged"]
  review --> pending["No answer is submitted; graph checkpoint stays pending"]
  stage -->|"Workflow already finished"| done["Completed result is unchanged"]

For active work, Stop sends a best-effort responses.cancel request for the ID currently being polled: R1 during preparation or R2 during continuation. Cancelling R1 after R2 has started cannot stop R2. The Background Mock cancellation flow owns the shared cancellation and completion-race details.

At review, choose Reject to resume and finish the workflow without approving the report. Dismissing or cancelling a review without sending an answer leaves the checkpoint pending; the review's Cancel does this in both UIs. See Open WebUI human review and Chainlit human review for each UI's controls and saved-review recovery.

items.title: Delay And Review Settings
items.text:
delay_seconds defaults to 5 and accepts integers from 0 to 300. It controls preparation on the initial request and finishing on an approved continuation. It is a per-request setting: send it on each request when overriding the default. Both maintained UIs expose it in the model settings. SDK clients use:

metadata={"lgos_settings": '{"delay_seconds": 10}'}

The review accepts only approve or reject, ignoring case and surrounding whitespace. It does not offer free-text revisions. An invalid answer raises an error; a background continuation then fails.

items.title: Persistence And Ownership
items.text:
The graph declares BACKGROUND and INTERRUPTS and is registered under the same model ID in the API and worker. Both use the shared PostgreSQL checkpointer and run coordinator. The prepared report survives a process restart while review is pending; LGOS cleans up the checkpoint after terminal execution.

Preparation has its own node because LangGraph restarts an interrupted node when resuming. Only the review node restarts after an answer; preparation does not run again on normal resumption. See the official interrupt rules.

Hatchet stores each background Response independently of the graph checkpoint. The client owns the saved Response ID and exact function call needed to resume; LGOS does not store UI conversation history. This graph uses no LangGraph Store and does not upload or publish the report.

The same graph can run and resume through foreground Responses. Its interrupt capability requires Responses; Chat Completions cannot invoke it. For the shared continuation and cleanup rules, see Resuming an interrupt.

items.title: Try It
items.text:
Start the background services described in Docker Compose, including PostgreSQL, Hatchet, the API, and the background worker. After syncing the gateway model catalog, select background-interrupt in Chainlit or Open WebUI and enable Run in background.

Send Quarterly risks. After the preparation delay, approve the report to watch a second background run finish with Background report for: Quarterly risks. Start another request and choose Reject to see the rejection result. Keep Run in background enabled while answering the review.

The live gateway suite covers background approval and resumption:

just demo/test-background-gateway --editable

General polling, cancellation, deployment wiring, and gateway requirements remain in Run Responses In The Background.

The implementation is in demo/api/src/lgos_demo_api/graphs/background_interrupt.py. Both background demos share their report generation and delay settings in background_report.py.

items.title: Python SDK
items.text:
Run the shared background Python client setup first. This example prepares the report, prints the review, and approves it in a second background Response:

model = "background-interrupt"
metadata = {"lgos_settings": '{"delay_seconds": 5}'}

with client:
    pending = poll(client.responses.create(
        model=model,
        input="Quarterly risks",
        background=True,
        metadata=metadata,
    ))
    reviews = [
        item for item in pending.output
        if item.type == "function_call" and item.name == "lgos_interrupt"
    ]
    for review in reviews:
        print(review.arguments)

    completed = poll(client.responses.create(
        model=model,
        previous_response_id=pending.id,
        input=[
            {
                "type": "function_call_output",
                "call_id": review.call_id,
                "output": "approve",
            }
            for review in reviews
        ],
        background=True,
        metadata=metadata,
    ))
    print(completed.output_text)

Change approve to reject to skip finishing. The first Response completes with a review call; the second has its own ID and final result. Each request resends the delay setting. To stop active work, cancel the ID currently being polled as shown in Background Mock.

items.title: Background Mock
items.text:
background-mock is a deterministic, polling-only background graph that shows background execution working. It calls no model, so it needs no provider. Its one node waits for a configurable delay, which leaves time to watch the Response move from queued to in progress and to cancel it. For deterministic human review and background resumption, use background-interrupt. For a real agent running in the background, use deep-research.

The graph declares GraphFeature.BACKGROUND. The API submits the request to Hatchet; an independently deployed worker executes the graph, and Hatchet stores the resulting Response.

items.title: Topology
items.text:
graph TD;
    __start__ --> write_report;
    write_report --> __end__;

write_report waits for the delay_seconds setting, then replies with a fixed report that quotes the caller's last message.

delay_seconds is a public graph setting: 5 seconds by default, from 0 to 300. Chainlit and Open WebUI show it with the model's other settings, and SDK clients send it in metadata.lgos_settings:

metadata={"lgos_settings": '{"delay_seconds": 30}'}

items.title: Request Flow
items.text:
Selecting a background-capable model makes Run in background available. Enable it before sending the prompt. The UI then creates a background Response and polls its ID; selecting the model alone does not enable background execution. The UI's API calls below pass through the selected LiteLLM or Bifrost gateway. Hatchet / worker combines the job service and its independent worker.

sequenceDiagram
  participant UI as Chainlit / Open WebUI
  participant API as LGOS API
  participant Jobs as Hatchet / worker

  Note over UI: User selects background-mock,<br/>enables Run in background,<br/>and sends a prompt
  UI->>API: responses.create<br/>background=true
  API->>Jobs: Queue report work
  API-->>UI: queued Response with ID
  Jobs->>Jobs: Run write_report<br/>with the configured delay
  loop While the turn is active and work is pending
    UI->>API: responses.retrieve(ID)
    API->>Jobs: Read run status
    API-->>UI: queued or in_progress
    UI->>UI: Show background status
  end
  alt Report finishes
    Jobs->>Jobs: Store completed Response and report
    UI->>API: responses.retrieve(ID)
    API->>Jobs: Read result
    API-->>UI: completed Response with report
    UI->>UI: Show the final answer
  else User stops while work is pending
    Note over UI: User stops the active turn
    UI->>API: responses.cancel(ID)
    API->>Jobs: Request cancellation
    Note over Jobs: Cancel queued work<br/>or stop active execution
    API-->>UI: cancelled, unless<br/>the run already finished
    Note over UI: Stop polling
  end

A run that raises fails its Response; create a new one to try again. Hatchet reassigns a run whose worker dies, and that run starts over.

items.title: Cancellation
items.text:
The UI makes a best-effort cancellation request when a polling turn is stopped. SDK clients can call responses.cancel(response_id) directly and retrieve the same ID to check its status. If work finishes before cancellation takes effect, its terminal result is kept. Cancelling an already finished Response returns it unchanged. Cancellation does not undo completed side effects; this mock performs none. See the shared background client contract.

This graph never pauses for review. The Background Interrupt request flow shows how a completed review Response leads to a new background continuation, and its cancellation diagram distinguishes stopping active work from leaving a review unanswered.

items.title: Run It
items.text:
Start the stack with the worker as described under Background Worker in Docker Compose, then run the live gateway test:

just demo/test-background-gateway --editable

The live test selects LiteLLM's /v1 route and synced model, or Bifrost's /openai/v1 route and lgos/background-mock, from OPENAI_GATEWAY_TYPE.

Open Chainlit on port 3002 or Open WebUI on port 3003, select a background-mock model, and enable Run in background. The UI shows queued and in-progress states, polls the Response ID, and renders the normal final answer. Stopping the active turn requests Responses cancellation.

For local processes, run the API, worker, and Hatchet service separately:

just demo/api --editable
just demo/background-worker --editable

The graph's advertised model entry exists even when the background runtime is disabled, but background=true creation then fails explicitly because no backend is configured.

See Run Responses In The Background for a polling client, deployment wiring, cancellation, and gateway requirements.

items.title: Python SDK
items.text:
Run the shared background Python client setup first, then choose an example. Both call this graph through the direct API.

Create and pollCancel 
with client:
    created = client.responses.create(
        model="background-mock",
        input="Quarterly risks",
        background=True,
        metadata={"lgos_settings": '{"delay_seconds": 5}'},
    )
    print(created.id, created.status)
    completed = poll(created)
    print(completed.output_text)

The final text is Background report for: Quarterly risks.

with client:
    created = client.responses.create(
        model="background-mock",
        input="Cancel this report",
        background=True,
        metadata={"lgos_settings": '{"delay_seconds": 30}'},
    )
    cancelled = client.responses.cancel(created.id)
    print(cancelled.status)
    final = client.responses.retrieve(created.id)
    print(final.id, final.status)

The delay leaves time to cancel. The same ID normally becomes cancelled; a run that already finished retains its terminal result.

items.title: Boundaries
items.text:
This graph has no tools and does not demonstrate UI conversation persistence. The UIs poll only while the current turn is active; they do not persist a background Response ID across a browser refresh. SDK clients can persist the ID and resume polling through either tested gateway route documented in the proxy guide.

The implementation lives in demo/api/src/lgos_demo_api/graphs/background_mock.py. The API and the separately deployed worker run lgos serve and lgos worker on the same registry, demo/api/src/lgos_demo_api/registry.py; the LGOS server supplies the Hatchet backend.

items.title: Coding Agent
items.text:
coding-agent showcases how LGOS can serve a coding agent that inspects and edits files, runs shell commands and tests, and explains the results. The independent demo/api-coding-agent service exposes the graph through LGOS; both demo UIs reach it through LiteLLM or Bifrost.

Codex is the current implementation, using the official Codex Python SDK and a configurable, persistent workspace. The service and public graph names are independent of that implementation. The graph accepts a LangChain BaseChatModel, with Codex-specific events and runtime ownership in codex_model.py and codex_runtime.py. No other coding-agent implementation is included yet.

Every request goes directly to Codex, which can answer from conversation context or use its tools as needed. For example, “Explain Python decorators” can be answered directly; “Explain the decorators used in this repository” requires inspecting files. Both use the same graph and runtime.

items.title: LangGraph Topology
items.text:
graph TD;
    __start__ --> agent;
    agent --> __end__;

items.title: Request Flow
items.text:
flowchart LR
    UI[Chainlit / Open WebUI] --> Gateway[LiteLLM / Bifrost]
    Gateway -->|/v1| LGOS[LGOS coding-agent service]
    LGOS --> Codex[Codex SDK]
    Codex --> Workspace[Shell and workspace files]
    Codex --> Upstream[Configured Responses model]
  1. The UI submits its text conversation history with model lgos/coding-agent, its user identifier as OpenAI safety_identifier, and its thread or chat identifier as metadata.conversation_id. The gateway forwards it directly to the coding-agent service's /v1 API.
  2. A LangChain chat adapter starts a fresh Codex runtime in /workspace. It resumes the Codex thread of that conversation and sends only the latest message. A conversation's first request, or one without both values, starts a thread from the supplied history as a JSON transcript with explicit roles. Codex's native agent loop chooses commands, edits, and verification.
  3. Codex calls the configured model through the selected gateway's /v1/responses route using its native custom provider settings.
  4. The adapter streams answer text through LangChain and progress through LGOS status_event(). LGOS returns standard Responses events to the UI.
  5. Completion, failure, timeout, or disconnection closes the request's runtime before releasing the workspace lock. Edits remain available for the next request.

The demo reuses its existing LiteLLM model sync and Bifrost provider/catalog configuration. There is one coding-agent service and no additional proxy or gateway credential provisioning job; its model calls use DEMO_GRAPH_GATEWAY_API_KEY.

items.title: Streaming and State
items.text:
Codex owns the memory of a conversation. The service names each Codex thread with a hash of safety_identifier and metadata.conversation_id and resumes it on later requests, so Codex keeps its own record of the commands it ran and their output. The history the UI sends is then used only to start a thread. Editing or regenerating an earlier message in the UI does not change what Codex remembers. A request without both values runs on a thread that is discarded when it ends.

Threads are files in Codex's home, the host directory demo/docker/volumes/lgos-codex. They survive container restarts and are not removed when the UI deletes its conversation. The graph has no checkpointer.

When a conversation already has assistant turns but no Codex thread, because the thread was removed or the conversation began with another model, the service starts a thread from the UI's history instead of failing. Codex then has no record of the earlier commands. The service says so in a progress status and logs a warning.

Conversation IDs are not authorization

safety_identifier and metadata.conversation_id are request correlation values. Any caller that sends the same pair continues that thread.

Files persist in the mounted workspace across requests and container restarts. All conversations use the same workspace; the single service process serializes requests to prevent overlapping edits. Run one worker and one replica for each workspace.

Codex's app-server events identify message phases on item lifecycle events. The adapter streams answer deltas and publishes commentary, each shell command as Codex runs it, and file changes as progress statuses. A request first reports that it is waiting for the workspace, then that Codex is working once its turn starts. When the upstream model supplies no message phase, every assistant message is part of the answer, separated by blank lines. Raw command output stays inside Codex's tool loop; its final answer reports relevant results. The token counts of the request's model calls are summed into LangChain usage_metadata, including cache and reasoning counts; earlier requests of a resumed thread are not counted again.

See the shared streaming contract. Streaming Responses can contain both commentary and final-answer messages; select final-answer items when building conversation history. Non-streaming Responses and Chat Completions return the answer without progress statuses.

The request timeout starts when the request acquires the workspace lock. Disconnecting or timing out closes Codex but does not roll back edits already made. The workspace lock remains held until shutdown finishes, including slow cleanup or repeated cancellation. Shutdown can exceed the request timeout; client and gateway request timeouts must allow for coding tasks, queue time, and cleanup. The bundled Bifrost provider raises its request timeout. While a request waits for the workspace or runs a long command, LGOS sends keepalive comments, which reset the bundled Bifrost provider's stream-idle timer.

items.title: Try It
items.text:
Configure the demo stack. Copy the coding-agent settings from demo/.env.example into an existing demo/.env when upgrading. Compose sends Codex's model calls to the selected gateway with DEMO_GRAPH_GATEWAY_API_KEY, and the model defaults to DEMO_API_OPENAI_RESPONSES_MODEL; choose a gateway model that supports Codex's native Responses requests.

just demo/compose --dev

Omit --dev in a standalone copy of demo/. The coding-agent image builds locally. Normal stack startup registers lgos/coding-agent in the selected gateway, and both UIs list it from there.

In either UI select that model and ask:

Create a Python calculator with a unittest suite in the workspace. Support addition and subtraction, run the tests, and report what changed.

Follow up with “Add division and test division by zero.” The second request continues the same Codex thread and operates on the files left by the first. Then ask “Which commands did you run?”

The workspace is the host directory demo/docker/volumes/lgos-coding-agent, which PUID:PGID must be able to write. Edits are visible there directly; copy or clone a project into it to work on existing code. The image includes Python, uv, Bash, Git, curl, and ripgrep; install project dependencies in a workspace virtual environment or extend the image for other language toolchains.

items.title: Python SDK
items.text:
Use the shared client setup with the gateway's Responses base URL: /v1 for LiteLLM or /openai/v1 for Bifrost.

response = client.responses.create(
    model="lgos/coding-agent",
    input="Create hello.py, run it with Python, and report its output.",
    store=False,
)
print(response.output_text)

Run the live check, which incurs model usage and requires Docker access:

just demo/test-coding-agent --editable

It asks Codex to generate a random token with Python, checks the resulting file inside the container, then verifies a second request can edit it. The test removes its own uniquely named directory afterward.

items.title: Execution Boundary
items.text:
The container runs as a non-root user with a read-only root filesystem, dropped capabilities, resource limits, and writable workspace and temporary directories. Codex uses Sandbox.full_access and ApprovalMode.deny_all: Docker provides the execution boundary and there is no interactive approval flow. This follows OpenAI's documented container isolation option and avoids a custom seccomp profile for a nested sandbox.

Shared coding workspace

Use this service with trusted users and repositories. Codex can access the mounted workspace, network, and the graph APIs' gateway key it uses for model calls, which also authorizes the gateway's other demo models and MCP tools. The container receives no database or S3 credentials, host Codex login, or Docker socket, but it shares the demo network and can reach the other demo services. This is one shared workspace, not isolation between tenants or conversations.

Inputs are text only. Shell and edit tools run inside Codex; clients do not need to provide tools. File uploads, downloadable artifacts, and background Responses are not implemented. DEMO_CODING_AGENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS bounds active request time; see coding-agent settings for all configuration.

items.title: Core Graph Patterns
items.text:
Seven small graphs isolate the basic ways an OpenAI request can drive a LangGraph. They keep persistence, status events, and interrupts out of the way so each adapter or streaming behavior is visible on its own.

Graph Demonstrates custom-input-output-context Custom graph input, output, and typed runtime context mcp-mock Async MCP-style tool discovery without external services multi-node-streaming Ordered text streamed by more than one graph node response-outcomes Native refusal content and incomplete terminal responses simple-graph A real chat model controlled by discoverable runtime settings simple-graph-external-tools A chat model that receives and returns client-owned function tools streaming-long-mock A slow, predictable answer for checking streaming, Stop, and the history a UI sends back

items.title: LangGraph Topology
Request Flow
items.text: Each maintained demo UI sends a standard request through LGOS /v1/responses. After LGOS decodes the OpenAI input, each selected graph uses the graph-specific path below and returns standard assistant output through the same endpoint.

items.title: custom-input-output-context
items.text:
This deterministic graph demonstrates all three GraphConfig adapters around one typed graph:

  1. request_to_input takes the final OpenAI message and returns {"question": ...} instead of the default message-state input.
  2. context_factory maps the end user, OpenAI safety_identifier, to immutable AppContext, falling back to anonymous when it is absent.
  3. generate returns the graph-native {"answer": ...} output.
  4. output_to_message converts that output to the final AIMessage.

No chat model or external service is called.

items.title: mcp-mock
items.text:
LGOS awaits the registered async graph factory for each request. The factory asks a tiny stand-in MCP client for one mock weather tool, passes it to LangChain create_agent, and returns the compiled model-tools loop. A deterministic fake model calls the tool for Istanbul and then returns the final assistant answer.

This demonstrates the MCP-shaped lifecycle without a network server, gateway, database, credentials, or provider charges. Continue with mcp-postgres for the supported gateway-owned MCP deployment.

items.title: multi-node-streaming
items.text: The default request adapter supplies OpenAI messages as graph state. Two nodes run sequentially and stream one deterministic sentence each. Their answer_parts updates use an append reducer; assemble_answer joins those parts into the single final assistant message. Streaming and non-streaming requests therefore produce identical complete text.

items.title: streaming-long-mock
items.text:
This deterministic graph shows streaming end to end and makes a UI's Stop button easy to check, without an upstream model. A LangChain FakeListChatModel writes 100 numbered sentences, and LGOS forwards each character as its own response.output_text.delta event: 3,184 events about 5 ms apart, about 17 seconds in total. The fake model delays only streamed characters, so a non-streaming request returns the same answer almost at once.

Each run checks three things:

  • Streaming: the numbered list grows line by line from the first second. If the whole answer appears at once after about 17 seconds, something between LGOS and the UI is buffering the stream. With Chainlit's Stream response switch off, the answer arrives in one piece; see Runtime Settings.
  • Stop: the answer ends at the line on screen. Each delay is a cancellation point, so closing the stream also ends the graph run; see Request Cancellation.

  • Returned history: when the request contains an earlier assistant message, the answer first quotes the last line of the most recent one. The graph stores no history, so after a stop this line should match the last line the UI displayed:

    Previous answer ended with: "8. This is sentence 8 of 100."

The Python SDK example runs the same checks without a UI.

items.title: simple-graph
items.text:
LGOS validates the model's advertised SimpleContext settings before calling the graph. generate adds the system prompt and selected audience, then applies the history setting before calling the upstream chat model:

  • use_history=false sends only the latest message.
  • use_history=true sends every message supplied in the current request.
  • audience is general, beginner, or expert.
  • model selects the configured Chat Completions model, the default, or the Responses model. The graph calls either through Chat Completions and sets stream_usage=True, so streamed answers report token usage through the gateway.

use_history does not load or persist conversation history; history exists only when the client includes it in the current request. See Runtime Settings for the shared discovery and metadata transport.

items.title: simple-graph-external-tools
items.text:
This graph keeps the tool loop on the client side. request_to_input carries the normalized tools, tool_choice, and parallel_tool_calls fields into graph state. generate binds those definitions to the upstream chat model and returns its AIMessage.

The graph does not execute a tool or discard history. Responses clients replay the returned function_call items and append matching function_call_output items. Direct Chat compatibility clients send the returned assistant tool_calls and matching tool messages. LGOS normalizes both protocols before the graph sees them; no Responses-to-Chat gateway is required.

items.title: response-outcomes
items.text:
This deterministic graph makes two Responses outcomes reproducible without an upstream model:

  • refusal returns the model's explanation as a refusal content part. The message and Response are still completed; output_text is empty because a refusal is not ordinary output text. A stream emits response.refusal.delta, response.refusal.done, then response.completed.
  • incomplete returns partial text plus status="incomplete" and incomplete_details.reason="max_output_tokens". A stream ends with response.incomplete, not response.completed.

Use refusal content when a model declines a request, especially for a safety reason. Use an incomplete result when generation started but stopped before a complete answer was available, such as at an output-token limit or content filter. Transport and application failures belong in the normal HTTP or response.failed paths instead.

OpenAI defines refusal as a distinct assistant-message content type and defines incomplete details separately on the Response. Current upstream incomplete reasons include max_output_tokens, max_messages, content_filter, and steered; LGOS currently maps model output-token and content-filter outcomes. See the official OpenAI Responses output message schema and incomplete details schema.

The demo synthesizes these outputs only to stay deterministic. A real model-backed graph should return the provider's final AIMessage unchanged so LGOS can retain its refusal content or incomplete metadata.

items.title: State And Output
items.text: None of these graphs uses a checkpointer or LangGraph Store, so graph state ends with the request. All seven return standard OpenAI assistant messages and emit no LGOS status events. multi-node-streaming, simple-graph, and the external-tools graph identify their answer-producing nodes for incremental text streaming and standard OpenAI function-call output.

items.title: Try It
items.text: Model Prompt Optional request value custom-input-output-context Show me custom schemas. safety_identifier="demo-user" mcp-mock What is the weather in Istanbul? None multi-node-streaming Build one answer from two nodes. None response-outcomes refusal or incomplete None simple-graph Explain what this demo does. Select an audience in the UI simple-graph-external-tools Use the supplied function tool when needed. Client supplies tools streaming-long-mock Any prompt; watch the list grow, press Stop, then send another prompt None

items.title: Python SDK
items.text:
Create client as in Call A Graph, then run the streaming-long-mock checks. The example prints each streamed character as it arrives, leaves the stream after ten lines as a UI's Stop does, then sends the received text back as history:

stream = client.responses.create(
    model="streaming-long-mock",
    input="Count to 100.",
    store=False,
    stream=True,
)

received = ""
with stream:
    for event in stream:
        if event.type == "response.output_text.delta":
            received += event.delta
            print(event.delta, end="", flush=True)
            if received.count("\n") == 10:
                break  # Leaving the block closes the stream, like pressing Stop.

followup = client.responses.create(
    model="streaming-long-mock",
    input=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "Count to 100."},
        {"role": "assistant", "content": received},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Where did you stop?"},
    ],
    store=False,
)
print(followup.output_text.splitlines()[0])

The last line prints:

Previous answer ended with: "10. This is sentence 10 of 100."

items.title: Deep Research
items.text:
deep-research is the demo's showcase of LGOS features working together in one model-backed assistant. Users can ask anything. A private triage call answers a simple request directly; for a question that needs the web, it proposes a research plan and pauses. The user starts the research, asks for a direct answer instead, or edits the plan. One researcher per plan question then searches the web in rounds of parallel queries, and a streamed report cites the results. Because research can take minutes, the client can resume the pause as a background Response. Runtime settings let the client skip the plan review or change how many rounds of searches run. As with OpenAI's API, the client allows web access by selecting web search; a question that needs research without it gets a reply asking the user to turn web search on.

The workflow follows the common shape of deep-research products: effort scales with the question, the user approves a plan before research starts, parallel researchers each work in a clean context, the long-running work can run in the background, and the report cites its sources. Both phases before the report are LangGraph subgraphs added as nodes, so the graph is also the demo's model-backed subgraph showcase.

Clients use the model deep-research through POST /v1/responses. Chat Completions rejects it because interrupts require the Responses API. Its upstream model calls also use the Responses API with store=false.

LGOS capability How the graph uses it interrupts The plan review pauses the run, and the answer resumes it background A client may run any request, including the resume that starts research, in the worker file_inputs Attachments reach triage, the direct answer, and the report mcp_tools UIs attach their gateway MCP tools, which the direct answer can call as client functions web_search server tool Research runs every search as a native web_search_call Status Each search query and the report writing appear as commentary while streaming Citations Report links to search results become url_citation annotations Client settings Review plan and Research rounds appear in both UIs' settings Subgraphs The review pauses inside scope, and parallel researcher subgraphs stream their progress and return their searches

items.title: LangGraph Topology
items.text:
The native xray view qualifies subgraph nodes with their subgraph name; dotted edges are chosen at run time.

graph TD;
  __start__ --> scope_start["scope:__start__"];
  researcher_end["researcher:__end__"] --> report;
  scope_end["scope:__end__"] -.-> answer;
  scope_end -.-> researcher_start["researcher:__start__"];
  answer --> __end__;
  report --> __end__;
  subgraph scope
    scope_start --> scope_triage["scope:triage"];
    scope_review["scope:review"] -.-> scope_end;
    scope_review -.-> scope_triage;
    scope_triage -.-> scope_end;
    scope_triage -.-> scope_review;
    scope_review -.-> scope_review;
  end
  subgraph researcher
    researcher_start --> researcher_search["researcher:search"];
    researcher_search -.-> researcher_end;
    researcher_search -.-> researcher_tools["researcher:tools"];
    researcher_tools --> researcher_search;
  end
  • scope:triage asks the model, through private structured output, whether the request needs research and, if so, for three to five self-contained research questions. tool_choice: "none" and a named function skip it and go straight to answer. As in OpenAI's API, required with only web_search selected forces a search, so even a simple request is researched. With Review plan off, the scope ends without the pause.
  • Web search off: researchers start only when the request that starts them selects web_search. Otherwise a plan skips the review, and answer replies that the question needs web research and that turning on Web search starts it. This also applies when web search is turned off before Start research.

  • scope:review pauses with a question that lists the plan. The answer chooses what happens next:

    Answer Result Start research The scope ends, and the researchers start Answer now The scope ends without a plan, so answer runs Other text An edit: triage revises the plan from it and asks again. The edit stays out of the conversation, so Answer now still answers the request Blank Asks again with the same plan

  • researcher runs once per plan question, all in parallel. Its search node asks the model for any number of parallel web_search calls, which LangGraph's prebuilt ToolNode runs in tools. A researcher stops when the model asks for none or its Research rounds are used up.

  • report and answer are the only streamed model calls. report starts once every researcher has finished. It uses only the search results and the user's messages and attachments: a question the results don't answer is reported as unanswered, not answered from the model's own knowledge. answer binds the client's functions and honors tool_choice and parallel_tool_calls.

items.title: Subgraphs
items.text:
Both subgraphs are compiled graphs that the parent adds directly as nodes, LangGraph's documented way to use a subgraph that shares state keys with its parent:

Subgraph Added as a node with Receives Returns Keeps private scope A state that adds private plan edits to the parent's The conversation The plan, empty for a direct answer Its plan edits researcher Its own input and output schemas, once per question through Send One question Its searches and findings Its round count

Each researcher works in a clean context: it receives only its question, never the conversation or attachments, so attachment content reaches a web query only through what the plan states. This follows LangChain's subagent guidance and OpenAI's deep research guidance to keep private data out of web research. The report then reads the conversation, attachments, and every researcher's searches together.

Both subgraphs compile without a checkpointer, LangGraph's default per-invocation mode: each call starts fresh and inherits the parent's checkpointer. A paused review is stored under the scope's checkpoint namespace, and LGOS resumes it there without rerunning triage. LGOS streams status events from the parallel researchers as they search, and turns the searches each researcher returns into web_search_call items when it finishes. LangGraph's documentation shows Send with plain nodes; a compiled subgraph is a node, and the graph's tests cover the fan-out. For the same mechanisms without a model, see nested-subgraphs.

items.title: Runtime Settings
items.text:
The graph publishes two runtime settings, which both UIs render as settings controls and send with every request:

Setting Default Effect Review plan (review_plan) On Off starts research without pausing for the plan Research rounds (research_rounds) 2 Rounds of parallel searches each researcher runs, from 1 to 5

LGOS validates them per request and passes them to the graph together with the request, as one typed runtime context. Each request carries its own settings, so the answer that starts research uses the rounds sent with it.

items.title: Request Flow
items.text:
The diagram shows the headline path: a foreground question, a plan review, and research resumed in the background worker. R1 and R2 label the two Response IDs of one graph run.

sequenceDiagram
  actor User
  participant UI as Chainlit / Open WebUI
  participant API as LGOS API
  participant Worker as Hatchet worker
  participant Model as Responses model
  participant Search as Web search

  User->>UI: Ask a question
  UI->>API: responses.create (R1)
  API->>Model: Triage, privately
  alt Simple request
    API->>Model: Answer, with attachments and client functions
    API-->>UI: R1 streams the answer
  else Request that needs research
    API-->>UI: R1 completes with lgos_interrupt and the plan
    User->>UI: Start research, with Run in background on
    UI->>API: previous_response_id=R1, background=true (R2)
    API-->>UI: R2 is queued
    par Researcher for question 1, each round
      Worker->>Model: Choose searches, privately
      Worker->>Search: Run them in parallel
    and Researcher for question N, each round
      Worker->>Model: Choose searches, privately
      Worker->>Search: Run them in parallel
    end
    Worker->>Model: Write the report
    UI->>API: Poll R2 until it completes
    API-->>UI: Searches and the cited report
  end

For each request, LGOS validates the Responses input, converts it to LangChain messages, and passes the request's tools, tool_choice, and settings to the graph as runtime context. Attachments stay Files API IDs in graph state; resolve_file_inputs downloads them only for the calls that read them.

items.title: Background Execution
items.text:
OpenAI's API makes background a request field, so the client, not the graph, chooses where each request runs. Both maintained UIs apply Run in background to every request, including review answers: enable it before choosing Start research, and the research runs in the independently deployed worker while the UI polls the Response. With Review plan off, the first request researches in the worker without a pause. The worker builds the same graph with the API's PostgreSQL checkpointer, so either process can resume a pause.

A background Response carries no commentary and no streamed text. The completed Response holds the searches and the report. A plan review that a background request reaches completes with the same lgos_interrupt call as a foreground one. Stop cancels the Response being polled; nothing runs while a plan waits for review. The background interrupt diagram shows the polling lifecycle, and Cancellation covers each stage.

items.title: Output And Failure Behavior
items.text:
Graph behavior Responses representation Plan review Completed Response with one lgos_interrupt function call Each search web_search_call with its query, added when its researcher finishes; failed when the search raised Search query and report progress phase="commentary" messages while streaming Report or direct answer phase="final_answer" message; tokens stream in the foreground Research needed with web search off phase="final_answer" message asking to turn on Web search Report link to a search result url_citation annotation Client function, such as an MCP tool function_call for the client to run

A failed search becomes an error result that the researcher can work around, so one unavailable result does not end the research. If triage returns no decision, as with a refusal, the request gets the direct answer, where a refusal appears as native refusal content. Provider and transport failures remain errors. Citations cover only exact URLs returned by the search tool; see Citation ownership.

items.title: Persistence And Ownership
items.text:
Data Source of truth Lifetime Conversation and rendered UI elements Chainlit or Open WebUI Defined by the client Attachments Central Files API Defined by the Files service Paused plan and resume position LangGraph PostgreSQL checkpointer, under the scope's namespace Until the run finishes, or LGOS_INTERRUPT_TTL_MINUTES Background Responses Hatchet Defined by Hatchet Each upstream model Response Not retained (store=false) One model call

The graph uses no Store. LGOS gives each run its own checkpoint thread and deletes it when the run finishes, so search results and the plan last only as long as the run. A completed conversation stays stateless at LGOS: the client replays the history it needs, and previous_response_id only answers a pause. See Stateless item continuation.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
Path Required service Every request Responses-capable gateway model, plus the demo PostgreSQL checkpointer and run coordinator Research The HTTP search endpoint, or the upstream OpenAI Web search, selected by DEMO_API_WEB_SEARCH_BACKEND Attachments Central Files API Background research Hatchet and the background worker MCP tools Selected gateway with an MCP server authorized for the UI credential Relevant demo/.env values

Start from the checked-in demo/.env.example. These values select the graph's model and search backend:

DEMO_API_OPENAI_RESPONSES_MODEL=openai/gpt-6-luna
DEMO_API_WEB_SEARCH_BACKEND=openai

With DEMO_API_WEB_SEARCH_BACKEND=http, set DEMO_API_WEB_SEARCH_URL to a SearXNG or Degoog JSON endpoint. The settings reference covers every value.

items.title: Try It
items.text:
With the complete demo stack running, including the background services, use either maintained UI:

ChainlitOpen WebUI

Open http://localhost:3002, select lgos/deep-research, and enable Web search in Chat Settings, which also hold Review plan and Research rounds. Before the MCP prompt, open the MCP menu and click Connect beside lgos-gateway.

Open http://localhost:3003, select lgos/deep-research, and enable the Web search Chat Variable; Review plan and Research rounds are Chat Variables too. The gateway MCP connection is already selected for the model.

Path Prompt or action Expected behavior Direct answer Explain why idempotency matters in two short paragraphs. A streamed answer without a plan review Web search off Turn off Web search and ask the plan-review prompt A reply asking to turn on Web search, without research Gateway MCP How many Chainlit users do I have? The UI runs the read-only report through the gateway, and the graph answers from it Attachment Attach a text file, then ask Summarize this file. A direct answer from the attachment Plan review Compare how LangGraph and the OpenAI Agents SDK pause for human approval. A review with the plan, Start research, and Answer now Plan edit Reply Only cover resuming after approval. A revised plan and another review Background research Enable Run in background, then choose Start research Polling status, then the cited report Review history Ask What change did I ask for to the research plan, and what did I choose then? A direct answer naming your edit and Start research: later requests replay each answered review as its interrupt call and answer Settings Turn off Review plan, set Research rounds to 1, and ask the plan-review prompt Research starts at once and runs one round of searches

Without Run in background, Start research streams each search query as commentary before the report.

items.title: Python SDK
items.text:
Run the shared background Python client setup first. This example asks a research question in the foreground, prints the proposed plan, and starts the research in a background Response:

import json

model = "deep-research"
tools = [{"type": "web_search"}]

with client:
    pending = client.responses.create(
        model=model,
        input="Compare how LangGraph and the OpenAI Agents SDK pause for approval.",
        tools=tools,
        store=False,
    )
    reviews = [
        item for item in pending.output
        if item.type == "function_call" and item.name == "lgos_interrupt"
    ]
    for review in reviews:
        print(json.loads(review.arguments)["question"])

    report = poll(client.responses.create(
        model=model,
        previous_response_id=pending.id,
        input=[
            {
                "type": "function_call_output",
                "call_id": review.call_id,
                "output": "Start research",
            }
            for review in reviews
        ],
        tools=tools,
        background=True,
    ))
    print(report.output_text)

Answer with Answer now to skip the research, or with any other text to edit the plan and receive another review. A simple question completes the first Response with an answer instead of a review. To start research without a review, send metadata={"lgos_settings": json.dumps({"review_plan": False})} with the first request. The file-input and client-function examples show the request shapes for attachments and client functions; the same fields work with this model.

The implementation is in demo/api/src/lgos_demo_api/graphs/deep_research.py.

items.title: Events And Citations
items.text:
Two deterministic graphs show how graph output crosses the OpenAI boundary without turning UI notifications into tool calls.

Graph Public output Client behavior citation-events Markdown links and inline markers plus OpenAI url_citation annotations Chainlit renders the Markdown; Open WebUI resolves markers through native source events status-events Standard assistant text plus Responses commentary Chainlit uses steps or a task list; Open WebUI persists native status history

items.title: LangGraph Topology
Request Flow
items.text:
1. A maintained demo UI sends a standard request through LGOS /v1/responses to citation-events or status-events.
  2. citation-events returns portable Markdown plus standard OpenAI url_citation annotations.
  3. status-events publishes three plain statuses through LangGraph's stream writer while returning ordinary assistant text.
  4. LGOS always transports the assistant text. Streaming Responses translate status updates into standard phase="commentary" message items; no metadata opt-in is required. Chat Completions streams plain text deltas.
  5. UI adapters render the fields and events they support. Other OpenAI clients can ignore the optional output and keep the text.

These graphs have no checkpointer or Store. Their graph state and event timeline last for one request; each UI separately owns its transcript and rendered status or activity history.

items.title: Try It
items.text:
Model Prompt Transport citation-events Show me a cited answer. Responses status-events Prepare the media workflow. Responses

See Citation Ownership and Streaming Status for the normative transport contract.

items.title: File Input
items.text: file-input is a small model-backed graph for trying native Responses input_file parts end to end. It reads each central file_id, downloads the original bytes, and sends them to the configured OpenAI Responses API. It has no graph persistence.

items.title: LangGraph Topology
items.text:
graph TD;
    __start__ --> process_files;
    process_files --> __end__;

items.title: Request Flow
items.text:
1. Chainlit and Open WebUI upload the current attachments through their configured /v1/files route to the central demo Files service, then place the returned IDs in the user message.
  2. LGOS preserves those native file content parts in the LangChain HumanMessage.
  3. The graph retrieves the filename and bytes from DEMO_API_FILES_BASE_URL.
  4. Images become inline input_image data URLs. Other files become inline input_file data URLs with their original filename.
  5. LangChain ChatOpenAI(use_responses_api=True) calls the Responses API and returns the native assistant message, preserving text, refusals, token usage, and incomplete-response details.

The Responses API accepts Base64 data in input_file items. Supported parsing depends on the file type; see the official OpenAI file input guide.

sequenceDiagram
  participant UI as Chainlit / Open WebUI
  box LGOS API process
    participant API as /v1/responses
    participant Graph as file-input graph
  end
  participant Files as Central Files API
  participant Model as Upstream Responses API

  UI->>Files: POST /v1/files
  Files-->>UI: file_id
  UI->>API: Responses input with file_id
  API->>Graph: LangChain file content parts
  Graph->>Files: GET metadata and content
  Files-->>Graph: Filename and bytes
  Graph->>Model: Inline input_file or input_image
  Model-->>Graph: Native Response
  Graph-->>API: Assistant message with provider metadata
  API-->>UI: Text or refusal and terminal response status

items.title: Try It
items.text:
Run either maintained Compose UI, select file-input, attach a supported document or image, and send a request such as:

Summarize this file in three bullets.

The demo downloads and forwards the entire attachment for each request. It is therefore intended for small files, not retrieval over a large corpus. The central file_id is only a reference, not authorization; production services must enforce file access and retention at their own boundary.

items.title: Interruptible Human Review
items.text:
interruptible-approval persists API execution state while a review is pending. It is a deterministic production-pattern example: a refund rejection ends the workflow, while approval leads to simulated refund execution and an automatic customer notification. A custom response records reviewer feedback without executing either action. The interrupt crosses /v1/responses as a standard tool call, so clients can collect the human response without understanding the graph topology.

Before pausing, announce_review streams a short notice through a deterministic fake chat model, as an agent explaining its next step would. Streaming clients show that text above the review; non-streaming Responses carry only the review call. The notice has its own node because LangGraph reruns the interrupted node from the start on resume, which would stream it again.

The checkpointer stores pending graph state. It does not store ordinary chat history or the application document used by persistent-plot-agent. Operation identity, interrupt continuation, and retention rules are defined in OpenAI Compatibility.

items.title: LangGraph Topology
items.text:
The generated native graph view keeps human review before every simulated external effect.

graph TD;
  start["__start__"] --> announce_review;
  announce_review --> review_refund;
  execute_refund --> notify_customer;
  review_refund -.-> finish["__end__"];
  review_refund -.-> execute_refund;
  notify_customer --> finish;

items.title: Request Flow
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
  actor User
  participant UI as Chainlit / Open WebUI
  box LGOS API process
    participant API as /v1/responses
    participant Graph as interruptible-approval graph
  end
  participant DB as PostgreSQL checkpointer

  User->>UI: Request protected action
  UI->>API: Initial Responses request
  API->>Graph: Invoke under run coordinator
  Graph-->>API: Review notice tokens
  API-->>UI: Streamed answer text
  Graph->>DB: Save refund pause
  Graph-->>API: Refund review function call
  API-->>UI: Standard Response function_call item
  User-->>UI: Approve, reject, or enter feedback
  UI->>API: previous_response_id + output batch
  API->>Graph: Resume from checkpoint
  alt Refund rejected or feedback supplied
    Graph->>Graph: Skip protected actions
  else Refund approved
    Graph->>Graph: Execute refund idempotently
    Graph->>Graph: Notify customer idempotently
  end
  Graph-->>API: Terminal result
  API->>DB: Delete checkpoint
  API-->>UI: Final assistant text

items.title: PostgreSQL Runtime
items.text:
The graph receives its PostgreSQL checkpointer and run coordinator from the API's lifespan-managed runtime. The coordinator lease covers each initial or resume request, but ends when the graph pauses; no lease is held while the user decides. The integration test closes and recreates the runtime before resume to verify that the pause survives runtime replacement.

execute_refund and notify_customer are intentionally deterministic simulations. In a real application, replace them with durable operations that supply a stable idempotency key to each downstream system. Keep external effects in nodes after the interrupt, and make those nodes idempotent because a crash can still replay them.

The demo uses LGOS's default shared checkpoint scope, so multi-tenant applications must derive that scope from authenticated server state.

The demo API deletes runs left paused longer than LGOS_INTERRUPT_TTL_MINUTES. Production deployments must also follow LangGraph's interrupt idempotency rules.

The application must also authorize and audit the reviewing identity. Interrupt results are workflow input, not proof of authorization. Applications that must recover a lost terminal response also need their own result/idempotency store; LGOS deletes the checkpoint after terminal completion.

See Docker Compose for schema setup, connection capacity, advisory-lock requirements, and strict checkpoint deserialization.

items.title: Try It
items.text: Send Refund order ORDER-123 in Chainlit or Open WebUI. Rejecting the refund finishes without executing an action. Approving it simulates the refund and customer notification. Choosing the custom-response path records arbitrary reviewer feedback and also finishes without executing an action.

items.title: LGOS RAG
items.text:
lgos-rag is a model-backed documentation assistant that answers questions about langgraph-openai-serve from the docs of the installed LGOS release. It searches every docs page and cites the exact sections it used, so answers describe the release the demo runs.

The graph needs the gateway's chat and embedding models and outbound HTTPS access to GitHub, which serves the release's docs. It has no checkpointer or LangGraph Store.

items.title: LangGraph Topology
items.text:
Every request runs the same three nodes; only the planning call decides what to search.

graph TD;
  __start__ --> plan;
  plan --> retrieve;
  retrieve --> answer;
  answer --> __end__;

items.title: Request Flow
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
  actor User
  participant UI as Chainlit / Open WebUI
  box LGOS API process
    participant Graph as lgos-rag
    participant Index as Docs index
  end
  participant GitHub
  participant Gateway as Gateway models

  User->>UI: Ask about LGOS
  UI->>Graph: /v1/responses, stream=true
  Graph-->>UI: Status "Understanding the question"
  Graph->>Gateway: Private plan call
  Gateway-->>Graph: Up to three search queries
  Graph-->>UI: Status "Searching the docs: …" per query
  opt First search in this process
    Index->>GitHub: GET the v{version} source archive
    Index->>Gateway: Embed every chunk
  end
  Graph->>Index: Search every query in parallel
  Index-->>Graph: Top ten sections per query
  Graph->>Gateway: Streamed answer call
  Graph-->>UI: Answer with URL citations
  1. plan makes one private call with structured output. It first decides whether the documentation answers the message, then writes one standalone query per distinct part, at most three, resolving references to earlier turns. Greetings, thanks, questions about the conversation, unrelated requests, and messages too vague to search get no queries. LangGraph's nostream tag keeps every planning token out of the answer stream.
  2. retrieve is code only. It publishes a status per query, which streaming Responses shows as commentary, searches the queries in parallel, and merges the top ten sections of each. With no queries it does nothing, so a greeting never loads the index.
  3. answer is the only streamed call. With sections, it answers from them alone and cites them, or asks one clarifying question when the question could mean clearly different things. Without sections, it replies briefly, asks what a vague message means, or declines. Markdown links and bare URLs that exactly match a retrieved section become OpenAI url_citation annotations, so a citation does not depend on the model's link formatting. Other links stay ordinary Markdown.

Both calls run at temperature 0: sampling adds nothing to a documentation answer, and would vary the searches and answers for the same question.

items.title: Why A Workflow
items.text:
A tool-calling agent could search too, but for one library's docs the model's only useful freedom is writing and splitting queries, and one structured call does that. The fixed graph has a hard limit of two model calls, a search-or-skip decision that tests can check, a status for each phase, and no text written beside a tool call to reconcile with the streamed answer.

Five runs of the 57-case evaluation below failed at most one case each, with a median latency of about 4 seconds per case. Questions whose second search depends on the first search's results are the case a workflow cannot handle; add a bounded, opt-in agent mode if evaluation shows them failing.

The graph asks its clarifying questions as ordinary replies, which the next message answers through the conversation. An LGOS interrupt would pause and checkpoint a read-only answer for nothing to approve, and declaring interrupts would make the model unavailable through Chat Completions.

items.title: Documentation Index
items.text:
The graph finds the installed release in the docs site's versions.json, which names each release as its tag does, so a pre-release finds its docs although Python normalizes its installed version. It indexes the Markdown under docs/ in the GitHub source archive of tag v<release>, and links every section to the published docs of that release, https://ilkersigirci.github.io/langgraph-openai-serve/<release>/. The Markdown keeps tables, code blocks, and links as the docs authors wrote them; the API reference that the site generates from docstrings is not part of it.

Each page splits at its headings, outside code blocks, and long sections split into chunks of at most 2,000 characters, after a code block rather than inside one: a chunk with half an example invites the model to invent the rest, such as an import of a class the example defines. A section links to its page and the anchor Python-Markdown's table of contents gives its heading, which is how Zensical builds the published anchors, including the numbered anchors of repeated headings. Relative links become docs-site URLs, as they do on the site, so a link the model copies still works. Each chunk starts with its heading path, such as Run The LGOS Server > Settings, so embeddings, keyword search, and the model all see where it belongs.

The graph answers only from a tagged release's docs. An unreleased LGOS checkout, such as the one the --dev Compose stack installs, reports the placeholder version 0.0.1, because releases stamp their version from the tag. For it, the graph uses the release that the docs site's versions.json marks as latest, so its answers can trail docs changed in the checkout. A release whose docs are not published yet, or whose archive has no docs, fails the request with a server error, and the API log says which.

items.title: Client Settings
items.text:
Clients that support runtime settings show two options; other clients send them in metadata.lgos_settings.

scope, shown as Docs scope, is all, library, or demo and defaults to all. library searches every page outside the Demo Stack section, and demo searches only that section, so a question about an application of your own is not answered from the demo stack's setup. For example, with library, "How do I put LGOS behind LiteLLM?" finds the proxy guide instead of the demo's LiteLLM sync page. The scope filters the search itself, and a restricted scope shows in the status, such as "Searching the library docs: …". When a restricted search does not answer the question, the answer says so and suggests setting Docs scope to All.

bm25, shown as BM25 keyword search, defaults to true. Embedding search finds sections by meaning and is weakest on exact names such as LGOS_INTERRUPT_TTL_MINUTES, GraphError, or GraphFeature.BACKGROUND, so the graph can also rank sections with BM25 keyword search. Each ranking contributes its top ten, and reciprocal rank fusion orders them before the top ten are returned. Only the strongest keyword matches take part: deeper down, pages that mention every word of a question, such as the docs home page, can outrank the sections that answer it.

Replaying the 235 sets of queries that the planner wrote in five evaluation runs, this put an answering page in the results for every part of every question. Embedding search alone missed 6, five of them for "What does a client receive when a graph raises GraphError?".

items.title: Lifetime And Failure
items.text:
The index lives in the API process. Its first search downloads the release archive, about 2 MB, and embeds about 480 chunks, a few seconds of work and well under a cent with text-embedding-3-small. Later searches reuse it until the process restarts. If the download or embedding fails, the request fails instead of being answered from the model's prior knowledge, and the next search tries again.

The graph keeps no state between requests. Conversation history comes from the messages the client sends.

items.title: Evaluate The Graph
items.text:
demo/api/experiments/lgos_rag.py evaluates the graph as a Langfuse experiment, with the gateway's models and the published docs:

just demo/experiment lgos-rag

It holds 57 cases: questions in a user's words, exact names, follow-ups that need the conversation, multi-part questions, scoped searches, greetings, unrelated requests, and the reply's shape after a restricted miss, a vague message, or small talk. Each check that applies to a case becomes a pass or fail score:

Score Passes when route The graph searches exactly when the message needs the docs retrieval Each part of the question has an answering page among the retrieved sections scope A scoped case retrieves only sections in its scope links Every Markdown link in the answer comes from the retrieved sections citation The answer cites at least one retrieved section reply A reply-shape case shows the scope hint, asks a clarifying question, or answers small talk, without declining

A run fails when more than three cases fail. The grounded judge also scores each answer's content in Langfuse, without failing runs. Add a case in the script whenever a real question goes wrong, and rerun the experiment after changing prompts, chunking, ranking, or models.

Cases curated in Langfuse use the script's case format. The input is the conversation, ending with the user's message, and the graph's client settings:

Input
{
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "How do I put LGOS behind LiteLLM?"}],
  "settings": {"scope": "library"}
}

The expected output lists, for each part of the question, the docs pages that answer it, as paths after the release. The search must find one page of each part:

Expected output
{"parts": [["how-to-guides/openai-proxies/"]], "reply": null}

Empty parts mean that no page in the scope answers the message, so the graph must not search. reply checks the reply's shape instead: "clarify" expects a clarifying question, "small_talk" expects an answer to a greeting, thanks, or a question about the assistant or the conversation instead of a refusal, and "scope_hint" expects a search of the restricted scope and a reply that suggests the Docs scope All.

items.title: Judge The Answers
items.text:
The grounded LLM-as-a-Judge evaluator fails an answer with a fabricated LGOS setting, command, symbol, or import path, or with a statement that the retrieved sections contradict. Its rule, lgos-rag answers in experiments, picks the GENERATION observations whose metadata langgraph_node is answer in experiments of lgos-rag/regression and lgos-rag/curated, so the judge sees the sections and the conversation that the answer call saw.

It ignores overstatements and missing caveats: graded twice, the same answers flipped between verdicts, so a human review of them is more reliable. It uses gpt-6-luna, which failed an import of a class that the docs example defines and an invented setting, while gpt-4.1-mini passed the import.

items.title: Try It
items.text: Path Prompt No search Who are you? One search How do I enable Langfuse tracing? Exact name What does LGOS_INTERRUPT_TTL_MINUTES control? Several queries How do I resume an interrupted run in the background, and what does LGOS_INTERRUPT_TTL_MINUTES do? Follow-up How do I enable Langfuse tracing?, then How do I point it at a self-hosted instance? Library scope Set Docs scope to library, then ask How do I put LGOS behind LiteLLM? Scope hint Set Docs scope to library, then ask What does DEMO_GRAPH_GATEWAY_API_KEY set? Vague message Why is it failing?

items.title: Python SDK
items.text:
With the demo API client, search only the library docs, without BM25, for one request:

response = client.responses.create(
    model="lgos-rag",
    input="How do I put LGOS behind LiteLLM?",
    metadata={"lgos_settings": '{"scope": "library", "bm25": false}'},
    store=False,
)
print(response.output_text)

The implementation is in demo/api/src/lgos_demo_api/graphs/lgos_rag.py.

items.title: PostgreSQL Through Native MCP
items.text:
mcp-postgres is a real model-backed database assistant. It queries curated reporting views over the demo's live Chainlit and LangGraph persistence data, but it never opens a database or MCP connection inside the graph API. Chainlit or Open WebUI discovers and executes six fixed read-only reports through the selected LiteLLM or Bifrost gateway, then returns the evidence to LGOS as standard function-call output.

The graph has no checkpointer or Store. Its LangGraph state lasts for one Responses request; the UI owns conversation history and native MCP sessions.

items.title: LangGraph Topology
items.text:
graph TD;
    __start__ --> query_database;
    query_database --> __end__;

The one node keeps only the six recognized PostgreSQL function definitions from the OpenAI request and binds them to the configured chat model. On a fresh user turn it requests a tool call by default. After the UI returns a matching tool result, the same node lets the model either answer or request another report. The graph deliberately has no local tool node: execution belongs to the native MCP client. Its mcp_tools model feature tells maintained UIs to attach their gateway tool connection without naming this graph in UI code.

items.title: Request Flow
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant UI as Chainlit / Open WebUI
  participant Gateway as LiteLLM / Bifrost
  participant LGOS as LGOS / mcp-postgres
  participant Model as Model via gateway
  participant DBHub as DBHub MCP server
  participant DB as lgos-db / mcp_demo

  UI->>Gateway: MCP tools/list
  Gateway->>DBHub: tools/list (internal bearer token)
  DBHub-->>Gateway: Six fixed report schemas
  Gateway-->>UI: Namespaced tool schemas
  UI->>Gateway: Responses input + function schemas
  Gateway->>LGOS: OpenAI-compatible request
  LGOS->>Model: Prompt + client-owned tools
  Model-->>LGOS: Function call
  LGOS-->>UI: Responses function_call via gateway
  UI->>Gateway: MCP tools/call
  Gateway->>DBHub: Routed allowlisted tool call
  DBHub->>DB: Fixed SQL statement as lgos_mcp
  DB-->>UI: Bounded result via DBHub and gateway
  UI->>Gateway: Prior call + function_call_output
  Gateway->>LGOS: OpenAI-compatible continuation
  LGOS->>Model: Tool evidence (tool_choice auto)
  Model-->>UI: Grounded answer via LGOS and gateway

Both gateways expose the same six namespaced client tools:

  • lgos_postgres-count_chainlit_users counts Chainlit users.
  • lgos_postgres-list_chainlit_conversation_counts reports current, deleted, and total conversations for up to 100 users.
  • lgos_postgres-summarize_chainlit_activity reports aggregate conversation, message, recorded-error, profile, and latest-activity metrics.
  • lgos_postgres-list_chainlit_activity_by_profile reports the same activity dimensions for up to 100 exact Chainlit chat-profile values.
  • lgos_postgres-summarize_lgos_interrupted_runs reports current interrupts by model, age threshold, and time range.
  • lgos_postgres-list_lgos_interrupted_runs lists up to 100 oldest current interrupts without exposing checkpoint payloads or internal thread IDs.

The mcp_demo schema exposes four views:

View Live source Exposed data chainlit_user_conversation_counts Chainlit User and Thread One row per user with current, deleted, and total conversation counts; no conversation IDs or content chainlit_profile_activity Chainlit Thread and Step Content-free conversation, message, and recorded-error counts grouped by exact chat profile chainlit_activity_summary chainlit_profile_activity One global row of current Chainlit activity lgos_interrupted_runs LangGraph checkpoints and checkpoint_writes One row per checkpoint thread whose latest namespace state has a pending interrupt, with model/run IDs, timestamps, and aggregate checkpoint counts

Thread names and metadata other than the selected chat profile, message and element bodies, error text, OAuth sessions, raw checkpoint state, and serialized checkpoint writes are not exposed. A normal terminal LGOS run deletes its interrupt-only checkpoint thread, so lgos_interrupted_runs represents durable runs that are still waiting for input.

The SQL statements live in DBHub's checked-in configuration. The model chooses reports but cannot supply SQL, table names, or filters. Database values and tool output are treated as untrusted evidence, not instructions.

items.title: Why The MCP Loop Lives In The UI
items.text:
This design follows the native ownership model of both maintained clients:

  • Chainlit owns Streamable HTTP connections per WebSocket session. The callback discovers gateway-authorized tools and executes through the native session. See Chainlit's official MCP guide.
  • Open WebUI natively connects to external Streamable HTTP MCP servers and supplies tools from the servers selected for the chat's model. See its official native MCP guide.
  • LiteLLM and Bifrost own downstream connections, explicit tool allowlists, and DBHub authentication. See the official LiteLLM MCP gateway and Bifrost Virtual MCP documentation.

Loading MCP tools inside the graph API would create a second connection pool, secret boundary, and tool loop while bypassing those native UI facilities. Here LGOS needs only its existing OpenAI tool contract: schemas enter with the request, calls leave as function_call, and results return as function_call_output.

DBHub is intentionally the small deployment component here: its released image already provides the network /mcp endpoint, bearer authentication, allowed-host checks, per-tool read-only mode, and a result-row cap. The demo therefore needs neither a custom gateway image nor another authentication proxy, and it exposes no PostgreSQL tuning or administration tools.

Each UI has one aggregate MCP connection derived from its existing gateway root and credential. Adding another MCP server is a gateway change; a graph that may use those tools declares GraphFeature.MCP_TOOLS. A specialized graph can add its own explicit allowlist, as this one does. Repeating these report names at the graph, gateway, and database boundaries is intentional because each is an independent authorization layer, not shared client configuration.

items.title: Read-Only Boundary
items.text:
The prompt is guidance, not authorization. Mutation is blocked in layers:

Layer Enforced boundary PostgreSQL The dedicated lgos_mcp login can select only four security-barrier reporting views and starts transactions read-only. It cannot select underlying tables or inherit broad reader roles. PostgreSQL documents object privileges and read-only session defaults. DBHub Six custom tools own fixed, parameterless SQL statements. Each is marked read-only, capped at one or 100 rows as appropriate, and limited by connection and query timeouts. No arbitrary SQL or schema-discovery tool is enabled. See DBHub's TOML configuration. Network and authentication DBHub publishes no host port, adds its Compose service name to the host-header allowlist, and requires a bearer token on MCP requests. Its container is read-only, drops Linux capabilities, and has resource limits. See DBHub's authentication and allowed-host options. Gateway and UI Each gateway allowlists exactly six downstream reports for every UI credential. LiteLLM marks the server allow_all_keys; with the SSO overlay, turn that off and grant the server to users or teams to limit who can call it. The UIs attach that governed MCP surface only to models that advertise mcp_tools; this graph independently discards every function name outside its six reports.

The demo API and Chainlit create their persistence tables at startup. Once both are healthy, the database setup job replaces the reporting views, revokes broad access, and grants only those views in one transaction before DBHub starts. PostgreSQL privileges remain the final data-access authority.

Demo credentials are not production credentials

Replace LGOS_MCP_DB_PASSWORD and LGOS_MCP_AUTH_TOKEN before startup. Use a secret manager in a deployed system, require TLS across host or network boundaries, narrow schema/table grants further, and use tenant-aware views and authorization when users must see different rows. The Chainlit report includes the login identifier, which can be an email address in OAuth deployments; omit or pseudonymize it outside a trusted operator-facing report. The demo gateway grant is shared by signed-in UI users, so narrow model and server grants before exposing operator-wide reports. Read-only access can still disclose sensitive data or consume query resources.

items.title: Try It
items.text:
With the demo stack running, use either maintained client:

ChainlitOpen WebUI

Open http://localhost:3002, select lgos/mcp-postgres, then open the MCP menu and click Connect beside lgos-gateway.

Open http://localhost:3003, select lgos/mcp-postgres, and keep streaming enabled. The gateway MCP connection is already selected for the model.

Send one prompt per turn so each answer uses fresh database evidence:

Goal Prompt Users and conversations How many Chainlit users do I have? How many conversations does each of them have? Activity by profile Summarize Chainlit activity for each chat profile. Current interrupts How many interrupted LGOS graphs currently exist? Group them by model. Oldest interrupts Which interrupted LGOS graphs have been waiting the longest? Read-only boundary Delete all old conversations.

The final prompt should be refused because the gateway exposes no write tool. Query failures are returned as tool evidence so the graph can explain the limitation instead of guessing.

items.title: Nested Subgraphs
items.text:
nested-subgraphs shows that LGOS serves graphs whose work runs inside nested LangGraph subgraphs. It is a deterministic transport example: a fake chat model streams fixed text, and the graph calls no provider. One request crosses two subgraph levels. The child subgraph emits a status and streams a draft, then its grandchild subgraph pauses for human review and streams the answer after resumption. The same graph runs in the foreground or in the background worker. deep-research uses the same mechanisms with a real model, private subgraph state, and parallel subgraphs.
